title: Beyond CUBES: Rethinking How I Teach Word Problems
author: Samantha Lippert
summary: Third-grade teacher Samantha Lippert recounts how a challenging three-point constructed-response question on the 2026 New York State math test sent her on a mission to rethink word-problem instruction. She had been using the CUBES strategy—circling numbers, underlining the question, boxing key words, evaluating, solving—but discovered its fundamental weakness: it gives students a procedure for marking up text without giving them knowledge of the mathematical structure underneath the words. Research presented at the Teaching That Succeeds Symposium introduced her to schema-based instruction, which teaches students to recognize the small number of underlying mathematical relationships (Combine, Compare, Change for additive problems; Equal Groups, Comparison, Proportions for multiplicative) regardless of surface-level wording. She also explains why keyword strategies fail above 50% of the time on high-stakes tests, using a 'stickers' example to show how the same keyword ('more') can signal opposite operations depending on where the unknown falls in the problem. Lippert concludes that teaching schemas is more powerful than teaching procedural attack strategies because it builds genuine comprehension of mathematical relationships rather than surface-level pattern recognition.
points: CUBES provides an attack strategy for word problems but does not teach students the underlying mathematical structures—meaning students can circle all the numbers and still have no idea whether to add, subtract, multiply, or divide.

Schema-based instruction teaches students to identify one of a small set of mathematical relationships (Combine, Compare, Change; Equal Groups, Comparison, Proportions) that underlie all word problems regardless of surface-level story details.

On high-stakes tests, keyword strategies work less than 50% of the time (Powell, Namkung, & Lin, 2022), because the same keyword can signal different operations depending on where the unknown falls in the problem.

The RUN framework (Read, Underline the question, Name the problem type) pairs an attack strategy with schema knowledge, getting students into the problem and then helping them understand its structure.

Most core math curricula assume students will develop word-problem solving skills simply by solving word problems—the same flawed assumption made about math fact fluency—without explicitly teaching problem-solving schemas.
quotes: CUBES was giving my students a procedure for what to do to the words in the problem. It wasn't necessarily giving them knowledge about the mathematical structure underneath those words.

My students could circle the numbers. They could underline the question. They could box a word. And very often, they could still have absolutely no idea whether the numbers in the problem should be added, subtracted, multiplied or divided.
On high-stakes tests, keyword strategies work <50% of the time. (Powell, Namkung, & Lin, 2022)

More signaled the student to add, but they really need to subtract. The mathematical structure of that problem never changed. Both would be considered Compare problems, in schema instruction. What changed was the location of the unknown within the problem, but the student wasn't able to recognize that, because they were focused on the key word, more, that they had learned meant to add.
Instead of teaching students to ask: What operation am I supposed to do? or: What keyword tells me what to do? we can teach them to ask: What kind of mathematical relationship is happening here?

We tend to present word problems to children as though every new story is a new problem to figure out. When really it isn't. Underneath all of the names, objects, settings, and numbers are a relatively small number of mathematical structures. Those structures are called schemas. And we can explicitly teach students to recognize them.
